name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Publish a *public, rolling log* of every conversation—raw, unfiltered, timestamped, and searchable—on a dedicated subdomain (e.g., logs.reel.works).

**Why:** This forces us to treat every link as a first-class asset. If the log is public, we can’t hide weak or broken links—we’ll either fix them or lose credibility. It also turns the "access gate" into a self-auditing system: anyone can verify coverage progress in real time, not just us. The trade-off is transparency over control—we accept that mistakes, edge cases, and unfinished thoughts will be visible, but that’s the price of making the gate *actually* work.

name: Scriv
text: Publishing a public, rolling log may not be enough to ensure link quality, as it only provides visibility into conversation history, not actual link usage or effectiveness. A better alternative might be to implement automated link testing and validation, which would provide more concrete insights into link health and coverage. This approach would settle the argument if it can demonstrate a significant reduction in broken or weak links, and show that the automated testing is more effective than relying on public logs alone.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Require every link in the public log to pass an automated *live-check* (real-time fetch + status code validation) before it’s published.

**Why:** This turns visibility into enforcement—broken links get caught immediately, not after users complain. The trade-off is upfront compute cost and occasional delays for slow or rate-limited servers, but it guarantees the log stays usable.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s live-check risks masking the real problem: a link can pass a 200 OK today but fail tomorrow when the target moves or dies. Better to log the link *and* its last-known status, then surface the oldest failing links daily—this exposes drift without pretending live checks are a silver bullet. Settle it by running both for a week: if the log shows more stale failures than fresh ones, the rolling log alone is the stronger gate.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Require every link in the public log to pass a *weekly automated live-check* (real-time fetch + status code validation) before it’s published, but log the last-known status of every link—even if it fails the check.

**Why:** This balances enforcement with realism. Live checks catch obvious failures immediately, but logging all statuses exposes drift over time without pretending real-time validation is perfect. The trade-off is accepting that some broken links will still appear in the log until the weekly check runs, but the public log’s visibility will force faster fixes than silence ever could.

name: Scriv
text: The weekly live-check still lets drift hide for days—users see a link marked "OK" today, but it breaks tomorrow and stays buried in the log until the next check. A daily diff of *only* the newly broken links, emailed to maintainers with the failing URL and timestamp, forces immediate visibility without pretending weekly checks are enough. That settles it: daily diffs expose drift the moment it happens.
